newsitem.title: CHINA: Deng reforms create ill that could end party rule.
newsitem.headline: Deng reforms create ill that could end party rule.

text.p: Deng Xiaoping introduced ambitious market forces to China to safeguard Communist Party rule, but those same economic reforms revived an evil which threatens that very power -- corruption.
Graft has been the downfall of many a dynasty in China's long history, and there are few issues more likely to stir ordinary Chinese to anger than officials who dip their hands into the public till.

Chairman Mao Zedong swept the communists to power in 1949 on a wave of popular rage against the corruption of Nationalist Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek and oversaw the effective elimination of the centuries-old practice of squeeze.
For three decades just about everyone in China was as poor as each other.

But then in 1978, Deng took over the reins and launched his economic and open-door reforms that created the opportunities for ordinary Chinese to make money and for officials to abuse their position for personal gain.
In the early 1980s, Deng replaced Maoist egalitarianism with such slogans as "to get rich is glorious" -- and many Communist Party officials took it to heart.
They used the lack of a legal framework and loopholes in rudimentary economic controls to make themselves, their relatives and their friends rich.
By the early 1990s, corruption exploded as the economy boomed, growth soared and the race to get rich moved into high gear.
Resentment against corruption was a motivating force and the leading grievance in the 1989 student-led demonstrations for more democracy centred in Beijing's Tiananmen Square.
On May 31, just days before Deng sent in the army to crush the protests, he took up the student's complaints and fulminated against corruption in a meeting with senior party members.

"We have to accomplish some practical things to prove that we are fighting corruption genuinely, not hypocritically... I too am outraged by corruption," he said in remarks that underscored the problems of rooting out such an evil in a system where personal power is paramount.

"I often try to find out where there is any violation of law or discipline in my own family," he said. "We can always uncover major cases of corruption if we want to. The problem is that we are usually hesitant about handling such cases. So we end up losing the support of the people, who come to believe that we are protecting wrongdoers."
Deng blamed corruption on decadent outside influences, and to an extent, seems to have accepted corruption as an inevitable side-effect of the economic reform policy.
When you open the door, he once said, flies and mosquitoes also fly in. Some people wondered why the fly-screens were not made a bit stronger.
"Corruption became a serious problem especially in the late 1980s when Deng was gradually withdrawing from politics," said a professor of economics at Shanghai's Fudan University.
"To the extent that he addressed the issue at all, he simply drew attention to it, rather than doing anything to solve it."

"After all the political struggle, Deng wanted economic development," said an analyst with the Shanghai Academy of Social Sciences. "His experience urged him to stress development over everything else. It was one of his blind spots."
Senior Communist Party officials have regularly said over the years that the fight to weed out corruption from among its ranks is of life-and-death significance for the party.

But rightly or wrongly, many Chinese believe that senior officials who misuse their position to the benefit of themselves and their relatives are left untouched because of their political power and connections.
There is talk of overseas bank accounts and of "princelings", the children of senior officials who make use of their parents' names to do highly profitable deals.
People see the luxury cars used by many officials and wonder where the money came from.

"What Chinese people hate most is corruption by high-level officials," said a Shanghai office worker. The Communist Party talks so much about serving the people, and say their power comes from the people. But in fact they abuse that power."
The party regularly mounts campaigns against corruption, and occasionally a high profile leader is toppled and charged with bribery.

The most senior to date is the former Beijing mayor and politburo member Chen Xitong, rumoured for years to be corrupt, who was finally removed last year after the suicide of vice-mayor Wang Baosen during a $37 million graft investigation.
On his last major public appearance -- his trip to southern China in 1992 -- Deng made no mention of corruption, but instead urged a new round of economic development.
The result is that Jiang Zemin, the current Communist Party chief and Deng's heir is left with the task of fighting the battle that Deng left unfinished.

But Chinese political analysts say that while Jiang is undoubtedly sincere about wanting to root out corruption, the job will be harder for him because he has nowhere near the same prestige and standing that Deng had.
"They are serious about battling corruption, but there is a limit to how much they can do because of the balance of power between various leaders and groups," said one analyst.

With Deng gone, there is also a fear among some Chinese that corruption will become even more of a problem - the central government, the argument goes, will find it ever harder to exert its authority.
Hong Kong has the same basic concern.

One of the main fears of Hong Kong residents over its impending re-integration into the Motherland, is the likelihood that corruption will increase, and that mainland people with good connections will be basically untouchable by the law.
Hong Kong reverts to mainland control at midnight on June 30 this year.
The ultimate answer to the problem, one Chinese analyst said, is better salaries for officials and consistent implementation of the Rule of Law, no matter who your father is.
"People hear that a senior official has a salary of 1,000 yuan ($120) a month, and they look at the way he lives and the privileges he enjoys and they conclude he is corrupt," the analyst said.
"But if you give him 10,000 yuan a month salary and limit his privileges, they will believe he is straight."

How Deng's successors deal with the issue of corruption and abuse of privilege will be closely watched -- their success will be an indicator of Beijing's strength and of the likelihood of Deng's demise eventually triggering significant political shifts.
